podcast.body: This double album was created amidst Billy Corgan's bitterness and disillusionment regarding the band's portrayal in the media, leading to the group's breakup by the end of the year. The album's narrative centers on a rock star character named Zero, whom Billy Corgan based on himself. Zero renames himself Glass after hearing the voice of God, renames his band The Machines of God, and attracts a fanbase called The Ghost Children. The liner notes and web postings from that period include numerous references to glass and shards of glass. "Billy Corgan was pretty bitter in dissolution by how the band was being portrayed in the media, and the group itself would break up by the end of the year as a result."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Intended as the Smashing Pumpkins' fifth and final studio record in 1999, this project was envisioned as a giant rock opera song cycle. It revolved around a rock star named Zero (renamed Glass by God), his true love June, and their collective rise, fall, and redemption. Band members were to assume these characters, with live performances presented as theater. The album was abandoned before completion due to bassist D'arcy Wretzky's departure (or firing), Chris James Eha's disengagement, and the record company's reluctance to release another sprawling album, especially after *Adore* was a commercial flop. "Its proposed title was Glass and the Machines of God. Never heard of it? Not surprised... The best guess is that glass and the Machines of God would have been divided into two halves of 14 songs each."

podcast.body: This album is mentioned as preceding the band's major rupture, leading to a period of confusion for fans regarding the lineup changes. "después del machina que venía yo creo que la gran ruptura de la banda nos perdíamos yo ya no sabía ni quién estaba allí ni quién estaba allí ni quién entraba ni quién salía ni qué hacían ni quién hacían."

srcs.episode: Vuelven los Smashing Pumpkins... mas o menos

podcast.body: This album was released in 2000, collecting the "best material" from the abandoned *Glass and the Machines of God* project in an attempt to salvage something from the effort. It won a Grammy for best artwork and was promoted with an early viral online marketing campaign encouraging fans to decipher its themes and storylines, though the campaign was abandoned unfinished. Despite critical re-evaluation, it became the second lowest-selling album in Pumpkins history. "In the end, Glass and the Machines of God was abandoned. The best material was then collected into a record called Machina, the Machines of God, in an attempt to salvage something, anything from the effort... Want a Grammy? For best artwork."
